title: Working Memory Overload
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane explains working memory through the concept of 'chunks,' pointing out that a person who has automatised a fact (like pi = 3.14, or 4x4=16) gets extra working memory space 'for free' compared to someone who has to actively compute or retrieve it under pressure. He walks through two concrete mistake scenarios, a circumference calculation and a Four 4s puzzle, showing how working memory overload during an intermediate step (recalling pi, or skip-counting to find 16) causes students to lose track of earlier information (the radius value, or how many 4s they'd already used), producing errors that look unrelated to their actual cause. He then extends the argument to learning itself, not just mistakes, using a proportional-relationship task and an inequality-sign-flipping example to show how a student can avoid making any visible mistake while still failing to learn the intended concept, because all their working memory got consumed on low-level computation (division facts, number-line placement) rather than the higher-order idea the task was designed to teach. His central practical claim is that working memory overload is counterintuitive and easy for teachers to misdiagnose, since a mistake's location often has nothing to do with what actually overloaded working memory, and the fix in both cases is building automaticity (via retrieval practice) in the specific facts consuming the most working memory.
points: Kane's chunking framework explains why automatised facts (pi = 3.14, 4x4=16) free up working memory 'for free' compared to actively computing or retrieving them, directly linking fact fluency to higher-order problem-solving capacity.

His circumference-calculation example shows a student's radius value fading from memory while they search for pi, illustrating how working memory overload during one step erases information from an earlier step.

He argues working memory overload is counterintuitive specifically because a visible mistake's location often has nothing to do with the actual overloaded step, misleading teachers into practising the wrong sub-skill.

His proportional-relationship and inequality examples extend the argument beyond mistakes, showing a student can complete a task correctly yet still fail to learn the target concept if working memory was consumed by low-level computation instead.
quotes: Working memory is where thinking happens. One of the striking features of human cognition is that we can only hold a few ideas in our mind at once.
The key idea of chunks is that you get more working memory space "for free.
When working memory is overloaded people make mistakes. This might seem obvious but it's worth looking under the hood at how this happens.
This student also doesn't have a solid chunk for radius times 2 = diameter, if they had that chunk solidly in long-term memory when they first saw the problem they would get diameter = 6 "for free.
More interesting are situations where a student might not make a mistake at all, but they don't learn something because they don't have solid chunks in long-term memory.
Working memory is counterintuitive. It fools teachers because when working memory is overloaded we can't peer into a student's mind and see exactly what they are thinking about.
